newsitem.title: CHINA: China slams war history whitewash by Japan right.
newsitem.headline: China slams war history whitewash by Japan right.

text.p: Beijing called on Sunday for greater vigilance against resurgent Japanese right-wing forces, accusing would-be militarists of trying to whitewash Tokyo's World War Two history of aggression against China.

The 60th anniversary of the July 7, 1937 Marco Polo Bridge incident that sparked the full-scale Japanese invasion of China was a reminder of the need to keep a close watch on Japanese right-wingers, the official Xinhua news agency said.

Some Japanese were becoming increasingly active in attempts to deny past warcrimes against China, the agency said in a commentary bemoaning the damage wreaked on the nation by Japanese aggression between 1931 and 1945.
"Even today, a handful of Japanese are advocating reactionary militarist historical views in an attempt to reverse the verdict on Japan's history of aggression," Xinhua said.
"The right-wing forces may be thin in manpower, but their energy and influence should never be underestimated. Therefore they deserve high vigilance," it said.

The anniversary of the clash between Chinese and Japanese troops at the Marco Polo bridge in southwestern Beijing is the latest opportunity for China to air its suspicions of resurgent militarism in Japan and to heap propaganda pressure on Tokyo.
Fighting at the bridge, which followed Japan's occupation of Manchuria, grew into a war that raged across China for almost a decade.

Beijing has been eager to publicise events marking its war of resistance against Japanese aggression as a way to boost patriotic sentiment among its huge population and to remind Tokyo of its militaristic past.

Ever-sensitive relations between Beijing and Tokyo have been tested over the last year by rows over a disputed island group in the East China Sea and by Japan's planned revision of its security alliance with the United States.

The revision would give Tokyo its highest profile military role in Asia since World War Two -- an idea that causes deep disquiet in Beijing, which would rather Japan remain an economic giant but economic and military dwarf.
China did not want to use historical issues to pick on Japan, but was forced to speak out because of the futile attempts of some Japanese to hide their nation's imperial past, Xinhua said.
"The monstrous crime that Japanese militarists committed in China... will by no means disappear with the mere disavowals of a handful of Japanese," it said.

"The more they try to cover it up, the more the crime will be exposed. What the small group of Japanese are doing will only make the already shameful historical records of Japan all the more disgusting," it said.
